Sorry
SOR-ee
adj.
From Old English sarig, feeling pain, from sar, sore; unrelated to sorrow despite the modern association. Webster 1828: grieved for the loss of some good; pained for some evil; also, poor, mean, vile, as a sorry excuse. The Authorized Version uses the first sense, and Paul builds a whole doctrine of repentance on it.

Biblical Definition

Sorry in the Authorized Version means grieved, and 2 Corinthians 7 is the passage that gives it doctrinal weight. Paul had written a severe letter, and he reflects on it with unusual candour: though I made you sorry with a letter, I do not repent, though I did repent: for I perceive that the same epistle hath made you sorry, though it were but for a season (2 Corinthians 7:8). He then distinguishes what happened next: I rejoice, not that ye were made sorry, but that ye sorrowed to repentance: for ye were made sorry after a godly manner (7:9), and states the principle that has governed Reformed pastoral practice ever since — godly sorrow worketh repentance to salvation not to be repented of: but the sorrow of the world worketh death (7:10). Two sorrows, one leading to life and one to death, distinguished not by intensity but by direction. Herod supplies the counter-example in a single line: hearing the request for John’s head, the king was sorry: nevertheless for the oath’s sake, and them which sat with him at meat, he commanded it to be given her (Matthew 14:9). Real grief, no repentance, murder committed anyway. And Nehemiah forbids the wrong sorrow on a day of covenant renewal: neither be ye sorry; for the joy of the LORD is your strength.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines SORRY as grieved for the loss of some good, or pained for some evil; and, in a second sense, poor, mean, vile, worthless — as a sorry fellow. Only the first sense appears in the Authorized Version.

expand to see more

SORRY, a. — Grieved for the loss of some good; pained for some evil that has happened.

Melancholy; dismal; as, a sorry sight.

Poor; mean; vile; worthless; as, a sorry excuse, a sorry fellow.

Webster notes the word is from the Saxon sarig, from sar, sore, and is not from sorrow, with which it is commonly confounded.

The modern conversational use of sorry as an apology is a late development and is not the biblical sense at all.

Key Scripture

2 Corinthians 7:8 — "For though I made you sorry with a letter, I do not repent, though I did repent: for I perceive that the same epistle hath made you sorry, though it were but for a season."

2 Corinthians 7:9 — "Now I rejoice, not that ye were made sorry, but that ye sorrowed to repentance: for ye were made sorry after a godly manner, that ye might receive damage by us in nothing."

2 Corinthians 7:10 — "For godly sorrow worketh repentance to salvation not to be repented of: but the sorrow of the world worketh death."

Matthew 14:9 — "And the king was sorry: nevertheless for the oath’s sake, and them which sat with him at meat, he commanded it to be given her."

Nehemiah 8:10 — "Then he said unto them, Go your way, eat the fat, and drink the sweet, and send portions unto them for whom nothing is prepared: for this day is holy unto our Lord: neither be ye sorry; for the joy of the LORD is your strength."

Modern Corruption

The reduction of repentance to an apology is the defining pastoral corruption of the age, and 2 Corinthians 7:10 is the text that dismantles it: two sorrows, one working salvation and one working death.

expand to see more

The public apology has become a genre with recognizable conventions: regret expressed, harm acknowledged, feelings validated, and nothing whatever changed. Paul’s test is different. He lists what godly sorrow produced in Corinth — carefulness, clearing of themselves, indignation, fear, vehement desire, zeal, revenge — seven fruits, every one of them active. Worldly sorrow produces feeling and stops there, and Paul says it works death. The difference is not that one grief is deeper. Judas felt more than Peter did, went out, confessed openly that he had betrayed innocent blood, returned the money, and hanged himself. Esau sought the blessing carefully with tears and found no place of repentance. Sorrow that terminates on the sinner’s own distress has nowhere to go.

Herod is the shortest case study in Scripture. The king was sorry, and then he had John beheaded to save face in front of his guests. His grief was genuine, his conscience was working, and it moved nothing, because the pressure of the company at his table outweighed it. That is worldly sorrow in one verse, and it names the mechanism precisely: the fear of man. Paul’s converse comfort is that godly sorrow leads to a repentance not to be repented of — a turning no one ever regrets afterward. And Nehemiah shows the limit: on the day the law was read and the people wept, they were told not to be sorry, because the joy of the LORD was their strength. Conviction has a purpose and a terminus, and the terminus is joy.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek lupeo (G3076), to grieve or make sorrowful, and lupe (G3077), sorrow, in 2 Corinthians 7; the English word is from Old English sarig, sore.

expand to see more

Greek lupeo (G3076) — to grieve, to make sorry; used five times in 2 Corinthians 7:8-11.

Greek lupe (G3077) — sorrow, grief; godly sorrow and the sorrow of the world are the same noun with different qualifiers.

Greek metanoia (G3341) — repentance, a change of mind; what godly sorrow works.

Greek ametameletos (G278) — not to be repented of, not regretted; repentance to salvation not to be repented of.

Old English sarig, from sar, sore — the English word is unrelated to sorrow, which comes from sorg, care.

Usage

"Godly sorrow worketh repentance to salvation (2 Corinthians 7:10) — the distinction the whole doctrine rests on."

"The king was sorry: nevertheless… he commanded it (Matthew 14:9) — grief that changed nothing."

"Neither be ye sorry; for the joy of the LORD is your strength (Nehemiah 8:10) — conviction has a terminus."
